extracted.intended_audience: researchers, authors, editors and stakeholders interested in peer-review policy and journal processes (particularly eLife authors and editors)
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and reporting of metrics used to evaluate a trial peer-review process at a single journal (eLife), including decision outcomes, timings, reviewer behaviour, and demographic subgroup comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouragement rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentage of initial submissions that were encouraged to full submission (invited for in-depth peer review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported for trial and regular processes (e.g. 70 of 313 trial submissions = 22.4%). Analysis should exclude initial submissions that were new versions of manuscripts previously submitted to and rejected by eLife (these inflate the regular-process encouragement rate). Encouragement rates are also reported by career stage (early/mid/late). Figures 1A–1C and Table 1 give breakdowns and note how excluding previously rejected manuscripts alters interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentage of full submissions that were invited to revise (i.e. received a 'revise' decision after peer review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported separately for regular and trial processes (e.g. in the regular process 58% of full submissions (94/162) were invited for revisions; in the trial all 70 full submissions ended with revise decisions). Table 1 shows revise rates by career stage. Interpret with sample-size caution where counts are small.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimated acceptance rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of all submissions that are ultimately accepted for publication (estimated from observed outcomes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported estimates: trial process ~22.4% (70/313) versus regular process ~15.3% (94/616). These estimates may be affected by withdrawn manuscripts and by outcomes of appeals; reported rates are tentative and likely to change with further follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision outcomes (before and after peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distribution of editorial decisions at the initial submission stage and after in-depth peer review (e.g., encouraged/rejected at initial stage; accept/revise/reject/withdraw after review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figure 2 shows counts and proportions for each decision category in regular and trial processes. In the regular process some papers were accepted after review without revisions and some withdrawn; in the trial process all papers sent for in-depth review ended with revise decisions (because trial papers cannot be rejected after peer review). Use both stages (initial and post-review) when comparing processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentage of rejection decisions that were appealed (including appeals before and after review where applicable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trial process cannot reject after peer review (so no post-review appeals in the trial), and authors may instead withdraw. Reported values: 5.6% of initial-submission rejection decisions in the trial were appealed, compared with 4.4% of rejection decisions in the regular process (counting both before- and after-review appeals in the regular process). Interpret differences keeping process constraints in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time to first decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Median time (and IQR) from submission to the first editorial decision (initial decision).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Previously reported medians: trial = 6 days (IQR 3–12), regular = 4 days (IQR 2–8). Use IQRs and consider seasonal effects (many reviews started in July/August) and unfamiliarity with the trial process when interpreting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time to decision after peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Median time (and IQR) from full submission (after encouragement) to the decision sent to the author following peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported medians: trial = 42 days (IQR 30–53), regular = 39 days (IQR 29–48). For revise decisions specifically, regular process median = 41 days (IQR 31–51). Single outliers (accepted without revisions or withdrawn) may be excluded from some analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer agreement and completion rate
rubrics_metrics.description: Likelihood that an invited reviewer will agree to review and subsequently submit a review (percentage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported overall rates: regular process 46.2% (47.9% for rejected papers, 45% for revise decisions), trial process 44.9%. Compare by decision outcome because reviewer behaviour differs for manuscripts that are ultimately rejected vs revised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer willingness to share name with authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of reviewers who agreed to reveal their names to authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported values: regular process 36.8% overall, trial process 42.3% overall. Breakdown by decision outcome: in the regular process 39.8% of reviewers shared their name for revise decisions but only 32.8% revealed their name for papers rejected after review. Consider decision-dependent differences when assessing transparency effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers contacted per paper (workload)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean (and standard deviation) number of reviewers invited/contacted per paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 2 reports means and SDs by submission and decision type (e.g., regular reject full submission mean = 6.08 (SD 2.96); trial revise full submission mean = 6.24 (SD 3.21)). Use these to assess reviewer-solicitation effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviews submitted per paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean (and standard deviation) number of submitted reviews per paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 2 provides values (e.g., regular combined 2.82 (SD 0.49), trial 2.80 (SD 0.47)). Use with caution — reported to two decimal places and given as sample means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers named per paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Mean (and standard deviation) number of reviewers per paper who revealed their names to authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 2 reports values by decision type (e.g., regular combined mean = 1.04 (SD 0.85), trial mean = 1.19 (SD 0.98)). Use to evaluate transparency effects of the trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer consultation comments per paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Average number (and standard deviation) of reviewer consultation comments per paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 2 reports values (e.g., regular combined 6.29 (SD 4.50), trial 5.9 (SD 5.55)). These reflect inter-reviewer discussion activity and can be compared across processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender-based outcome comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis of submission and decision outcomes by gender of the last author (percentages and revise rates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported: among reviewed submissions the regular process had 78.2% male and 21.8% female last authors; trial 78.6% male and 21.4% female. In the regular process, revise rate for male last authors = 53.2% (67/126) vs female last authors = 74.3% (26/35), but note small sample size for female last-authored papers in the regular review set. Compare with larger external studies (e.g., Murray et al.) and interpret cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Career-stage-based outcome comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis of encouragement, review and decision outcomes by career stage of the last author (early, mid, late), with explicit career-stage definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Career-stage definitions used: early = ≤5 years independent; mid = 6–15 years; late = >15 years. Reported patterns: earlier analyses suggested higher encouragement for late-career authors; after excluding previously rejected resubmissions the differences between early- and late-career encouragement rates are reduced though mid-career still differs. Revise rates can be higher for early-career manuscripts; Table 1 and Figures 1/5 present the breakdowns. The team contacted authors to complete missing career-stage data and excluded previously considered manuscripts from further analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion criterion for prior-rejected resubmissions in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic rule to exclude initial submissions that were previously submitted to eLife and rejected from comparisons between trial and regular processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: previously rejected resubmissions have higher-than-average encouragement rates because authors have responded to prior reviewer concerns; including them inflates the regular-process encouragement rate. The original regular sample included 49 such manuscripts and analyses were updated after excluding them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial process publication commitment and author control
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy rule: in the trial, once a paper is invited for peer review the journal is committed to publishing the work (and the peer review assessments) unless the authors choose to withdraw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structural difference affects outcome measures (e.g., no post-review rejections in the trial, different appeal behaviour). Authors retain control of the ultimate decision and may withdraw rather than accept an editorial rejection after review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical and interpretive caveats (sample-size and time effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance to interpret results cautiously due to small sample sizes in some subgroups and possible time-period effects on review times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly cautions that numbers of manuscripts (especially in subgroup analyses by gender or career stage) are relatively small, which limits confidence in some observations. Additionally, review times may have been longer because many reviews were started in July/August and because editors were less familiar with the trial process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planned operational interventions to address disparities
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed changes to editorial practice intended to reduce observed disparities (recruitment and process changes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Planned initiatives include recruiting more early- and mid-career researchers to the Board of Reviewing Editors; collecting career-stage information at submission to permit longer-term monitoring; and exploring a trial in which author names are not made available to editors during the initial evaluation. These are presented as response measures rather than scored metrics.
